segments.text: Jurisdiction is the legal authority of a state to prescribe rules, adjudicate disputes and enforce law.
Study territorial jurisdiction first, then nationality, passive personality, protective and universal jurisdiction. Enforcement jurisdiction is especially sensitive when exercised beyond territory.

State jurisdiction can be divided into prescriptive jurisdiction, adjudicative jurisdiction and enforcement jurisdiction. Prescriptive jurisdiction concerns authority to make law applicable to conduct or persons. Adjudicative jurisdiction concerns authority of courts or tribunals to decide cases. Enforcement jurisdiction concerns coercive implementation, such as arrest or seizure.

These dimensions can point in different directions. A state may have a legal basis to criminalize certain conduct abroad yet still lack authority to send its police into another state's territory without consent or another recognized legal basis.

Territorial jurisdiction is the normal starting point. Nationality jurisdiction permits regulation of nationals in circumstances recognized by international law. Passive personality links jurisdiction to nationality of the victim. The protective principle addresses conduct threatening essential state interests. Universal jurisdiction is claimed for a limited category of offences considered of concern to the international community, subject to legal controversy and domestic implementation.

Extraterritorial jurisdiction should always be connected to a recognized basis and to principles of reasonableness, comity or treaty limitation where relevant. Labels alone do not settle every jurisdictional conflict.

Enforcement is the most sovereignty-sensitive category. Physical police action, search, arrest or seizure in foreign territory ordinarily requires consent, treaty authority or another valid legal basis. Mutual legal assistance and extradition exist precisely because cross-border enforcement cannot normally be conducted unilaterally.

items.text: prescriptive jurisdiction to make rules, adjudicative jurisdiction to decide cases, and enforcement jurisdiction to compel compliance.
Territoriality is the normal starting point because states have primary authority over conduct in their territory. Nationality jurisdiction connects a state to its nationals abroad.
Other bases may include passive personality, protective jurisdiction and universal jurisdiction in recognized circumstances. Each basis has its own legal rationale and limits.
Enforcement abroad is especially restricted because physically exercising state power in another state's territory can infringe sovereignty unless international law or consent permits it.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not treat a valid basis to prescribe law as automatic permission to send police or enforcement officers into another state.
